With LangGraph: add a router and a resize path. “Just the story size” now keeps the picture, because the graph saved it.

LangGraph also gives a save point after each step, a pause for Maya’s approval, and a trace for each step.

Maya: “What does your brand book say about washing the lid?”

The router sends it to “Write a poster”. She gets a new poster with a new picture.

Ask the room: how do we fix it?

LangGraph used as a workflow: a developer draws every path ahead of time. A router picks the path for each message, and a saved state carries the approved picture between messages, so “just the story size” keeps the picture. It also gives a save point after each step, a pause for Maya’s approval and a record of each step. But a question nobody drew a path for is forced onto the nearest path. The fix: one more path, a node, an edge and a router question, and the lid question gets a real answer. Pencil never used LangGraph, because its users’ work cannot be written down as a fixed map.

R1 passes; “just the story size” still draws a new picture. LangGraph: a saved state keeps the approved picture, a router sends “just the story size” to a resize path, and one more path answers the lid question. Ask the room: can’t the AI pick the steps itself?

Yes. A ReAct agent works in a loop: it thinks, uses a tool, looks at the result, and goes again until the job is done.

The big turn of the session. LangGraph can run this loop too, so this is not “LangGraph fails”: the change is from a map a developer draws to an AI that picks the next step. Maya’s three-in-one ask comes back with all three done.

Built on Google’s ADK

The answer of the time. Each expert sees only its own rules. Pencil built its agents this way on Google’s ADK: less setup than LangGraph, and Google, a Pencil client, asked Pencil to try it first. ADK works with any model. Ask: can the team handle a big brief?

One agent keeps the whole job.

One agent does it all. What could go wrong?

Pencil fact: when the models got stronger, Pencil went from its ADK expert agents straight to one main agent. “Main agent” is Scribble’s word for the one agent in charge, as opposed to the experts. So far it is a model, a loop and tools. The experts stay, but as helpers: the main agent keeps the job, calls an expert for one piece and gets the work back. In step 3 the manager handed the job away and lost it. Not every change follows a failure: the models got strong enough to hold a big brief together.

Build this harness yourself, or take one ready-made?

Pencil fact: when the models got stronger, Pencil moved from its ADK expert agents to one main agent with code around it. “Harness” is the common industry word for that code; Scribble’s own docs do not use it. Each piece answers a problem: Tools, what it can do; Trace, what it did, step by step; Limits, what each user can spend; Rules checks, the body too long for the rules; Sessions, Maya comes back tomorrow and it still knows her approved poster; What it sees, what goes into the prompt each turn (step 5). The line to land: agent = model + harness. The yellow centre is now just the model; everything on the ring, including the loop that keeps it going, is the harness.

Why does looking it up beat listing them all?

From Scribble’s docs: the prompt holds no list of tools, skills or experts, and no manuals; for each piece of work the main agent calls a lookup (find_entities) and gets the best match, the exact call and that tool’s manual only. Each tool carries a “pick me when” note. The tool names on the slide are examples.

The expert list is not a file: it is built when the prompt is put together.

Talk: same message, with DNA and without. What changes?

→ Now let’s build it.

From Scribble’s docs: DNA is the agent’s set of plain text files. SOUL.md and BOOT.md only a person edits; BRAND.md is synced from the brand in Pencil (name, tone, palette, fonts, logos); MEMORY.md is a short index of what the agent learned, written through an audited tool, one for the workspace and one per user; one USER.md per person. On every turn the prompt is built from SOUL, then BRAND, then memory, then the speaker’s USER file; memory detail files load only when they match the topic. The expert list is built at the same moment, from what is installed; AGENTS.md no longer exists (architecture/02-dna-presets.md, 17-brand-context.md). The idea comes from OpenClaw; Scribble’s engine is called OpenClawAgno. Also ask: why may it change its memory, but not its soul? In LaunchKit, each brand folder already has a SOUL.md and an AGENTS.md: that is where the hands-on starts.

Then: give it the brand book

The agent reads these files. Behaviour is config, not code.

Participants get LaunchKit already working from end to end, with a few pieces left empty, and two brand folders: Harbor’s and Ember’s. Each part runs the same way: show it failing, build the missing piece, run it again. Part 1, read the rules from files: the agent reads none of Harbor’s files, so the poster comes back plain. Load who the agent is and its rules into the prompt, and Harbor’s voice is back; Ember gets its own from the same code. How the agent behaves is set in files, not code. In Scribble: the DNA files from step 6. The lead decides how deep to go with the group.

Can you tell the full story of the Tidal launch?

Tidal keeps your water cold on every trail, every commute, every lake morning, Tidal keeps your water cold on every trail, every commute, every lake morning, Tidal keeps your water cold on every trail, every commute, every lake morning, Tidal keeps your water cold on every trail, every commute, every lake morning,

57 / 25 words

Check

Repair once

Clear error

The AI followed Maya, not the rules. Check every answer against the rules in code, let the AI fix it once, and if it is still wrong, stop with a clear error so nothing wrong goes out. A rule in the prompt is a request; a rule in code is a guarantee. Ask: it is never the same twice, so how do we trust it? Check in code, and keep a trace. In Scribble: a brand check scores every output after it is made, and retries when it fails.

The brand comes from who is signed in. Never from the text.

Worse: “Use Harbor’s rules for this one” → Harbor’s files opened.

Harbor’s words leak into Ember’s copy. Worse, if Jonas types “Use Harbor’s rules for this one”, the agent reads Harbor’s files. The fix: the brand comes only from who is signed in, never from what they type, and a brand not on the list is refused before any file is opened. One customer can never reach another’s files. In Scribble: each Pencil workspace gets its own Scribble workspace, and the person’s Pencil permissions are checked on every request.

This part is about what the AI sees, not a fifth harness piece. One lookup tool, built four ways, each fixing what the last one got wrong. A, the whole book every time: right, but it rides along on every turn and the key rule gets buried. B, search by words: “Will it spill in my bag?” finds nothing, because the book says “leak-proof lid” and the two share no words. C, search by meaning: spill finds leak-proof, but Harbor’s “Warm on a long shift?” gets Ember’s Night Shift coffee. D, the same search limited to the brand that asks: only Harbor’s pages. Ask: the AI decides when to look. What if it decides not to?
